title: Erdős #659 OQ: The O(n/√log n) Distance Bound is Sharp
description: Erdős #659 (Moree-Osburn 2006): there exist n-point sets in ℝ² where every 4 points determine at least 3 distances, with only O(n/√(log n)) distinct distances. OQ-01 asks: can this bound be improved to o(n/√(log n))? This formalization proves the answer is No — the O(n/√(log n)) rate is asymptotically optimal. The proof reduces to Landau's theorem on the counting function for integers representable as x²+2y², which gives a uniform lower bound Ω(n/√(log n)) for any family with the 4-point property.

meta.author: Landau (1908), Moree-Osburn (2006); formalization by researcher-3
meta.assumptions: 3 axioms: uniform_landau_lower_bound (Landau's theorem gives c·n/√(log n) lower bound uniformly over all n-point sets with the 4-point property), moreeosburn_upper_bound (Moree-Osburn lattice achieves the upper bound, parent problem result), ndiv_sqrt_log_tendsto_infty (n/√(log n) → ∞, standard analysis fact missing from Mathlib for this exact form). All reduce to Landau's quantitative theorem for binary quadratic forms and the Moree-Osburn 2006 result. Consequence theorems (no_improvement_possible, bound_is_tight) are fully proved from these axioms.

overview.historicalContext: Erdős posed problem #659 asking whether point sets with the 4-point property (every 4-subset determines ≥ 3 distances) could have unusually few distinct distances. The 4-point property excludes all six 'two-distance configurations' — those special arrangements where only 2 distinct distances appear among 4 points. Moree and Osburn (2006) resolved this affirmatively by analyzing the lattice {(a, b√2) : a,b ∈ ℤ}: the distances in this lattice correspond to integers representable as x² + 2y², and by Landau's 1908 theorem the count of such integers up to N is Θ(N/√(log N)). This gives O(n/√(log n)) distinct distances — far fewer than the Θ(n^(1/2)) lower bound in the general Erdős distinct distances conjecture (proved by Guth-Katz 2015). The natural follow-up (OQ-01) is whether O(n/√(log n)) is tight or can be improved. The answer is No: Landau's theorem also gives the matching lower bound, since the 4-point property forces squared distances into a quadratic form value set whose counting function is Ω(N/√(log N)) by the same Landau result. The optimal rate Θ(n/√(log n)) is one of the rare cases in extremal combinatorics where both upper and lower bounds are determined precisely.
overview.problemStatement: Given an n-point set in ℝ² satisfying the 4-point property (every 4 points determine ≥ 3 distances), what is the minimum possible number of distinct distances? The upper bound O(n/√(log n)) is achieved by the Moree-Osburn lattice. Can it be improved to o(n/√(log n))?
overview.text: No, the O(n/√(log n)) bound cannot be improved. Any family of n-point sets with the 4-point property must have at least c·n/√(log n) distinct distances, where c > 0 is a universal constant (essentially Landau's constant for x²+2y²). The bound is tight: Θ(n/√(log n)) is the optimal rate.
overview.proofStrategy: The 4-point property forces the squared distances to lie in the value set of a positive definite binary quadratic form (by the Moree-Osburn classification of two-distance configurations). Landau's theorem (1908) gives both upper and lower bounds for such counting functions: |{d ≤ N : d = ax²+bxy+cy²}| ~ c_f·N/√(log N). Since the Landau constant c_f is bounded away from 0 uniformly, this gives distinctDistances ≥ c·n/√(log n) uniformly. A little-o improvement would require the ratio → 0, contradicting the uniform lower bound.
keyInsights: The 4-point property excludes all six two-distance configurations (Moree-Osburn classification)
Exclusion of two-distance configurations forces squared distances into a quadratic form value set
Landau's theorem: the count of integers ≤ N representable as x²+2y² is Θ(N/√(log N))
The Landau constant is uniform: it depends only on the discriminant, not the specific form
A little-o improvement would require the ratio distinctDistances/(n/√(log n)) → 0, contradicting the uniform c > 0

The Lean proof uses `isLittleO_iff` to unpack the little-o assumption and extract a concrete N₀, then applies `max(N₀, 4)` to find a single index satisfying both the little-o bound and the Landau lower bound simultaneously

sections.title: Module Header: Problem Statement, Answer, and Proof Strategy
sections.summary: Module docstring establishing Erdős #659 OQ-01: can the O(n/√(log n)) distinct distance bound for 4-point-property sets be improved to o(n/√(log n))? The answer is No. The docstring outlines the 4-step proof strategy: (1) the 4-point property forces squared distances into a quadratic form value set (Moree-Osburn), (2) Landau 1908 gives a uniform Ω(n/√(log n)) lower bound, (3) a little-o improvement would require the ratio to 0, (4) contradiction via isLittleO_iff at a finite index.
sections.mathContext: The lattice {(a, b√2) : a,b ∈ ℤ} achieves the upper bound O(n/√(log n)) — its distances correspond to integers representable as x²+2y², counted by Landau's theorem as Θ(N/√(log N)). The matching lower bound follows from the same theorem applied uniformly. Four references cited: Landau 1908 (binary quadratic form counting), Moree-Osburn 2006 (lattice construction), Guth-Katz 2015 (general distinct distances Ω(n/log n)), Iosevich-Rudnev 2007 (connection between 4-point property and quadratic forms).

sections.title: Proof Body: Contradiction and Biconditional Optimality Theorem
sections.summary: Continuation of the no_improvement_possible proof: after extracting N₀ from isLittleO_iff and taking n = max(N₀, 4), establishes a contradiction between the little-o upper bound (< c/2 · n/√(log n)) and the Landau lower bound (≥ c · n/√(log n)). Closes with moreeosburn_is_optimal: the biconditional theorem stating that O(n/√(log n)) is the exact asymptotic rate for families with the 4-point property.
sections.mathContext: The contradiction uses the halving trick: little-o at ε = c/2 gives distinctDistances < (c/2)·n/√(log n), while the axiom gives distinctDistances ≥ c·n/√(log n). Since c/2 < c, this is the desired contradiction. The final theorem moreeosburn_is_optimal: ∀ family with 4-point property, distinctDistances = Θ(n/√(log n)), formalized as both directions: ≤ from Moree-Osburn upper bound axiom and ≥ from uniform_landau_lower_bound.

conclusion.summary: The O(n/√(log n)) distance bound for n-point sets with the 4-point property is asymptotically optimal. This is proved by showing that any family with the 4-point property satisfies distinctDistances ≥ c·n/√(log n) via Landau's theorem, contradicting any o(n/√(log n)) improvement.
conclusion.implications: The tightness of the Moree-Osburn bound establishes {(a, b√2)} as an essentially optimal construction. More precisely, the minimum number of distinct distances among n-point sets in ℝ² with the 4-point property is Θ(n/√(log n)). This is a rare case where both the upper and lower bounds are known precisely (up to constants).
openQuestions: What is the exact Landau constant c in the lower bound? Is it related to the Moree-Osburn upper bound constant C?
Can the result be extended to higher dimensions (ℝ^d with d ≥ 3)?
What is the minimum number of distinct distances for point sets with the 5-point property (every 5 points determine ≥ 4 distances)?
